explain.title: When is work done?

explain.title: Work in the same direction
explain.body: When force and distance are in the same direction, use W = F × S. If an object does not move, its displacement is zero and no work is done by the force.

explain.title: A force at an angle
explain.body: Only the component F cos θ acts along the motion. Therefore, W = FS cos θ. At 90°, cos 90° = 0, so a perpendicular force does no work.

explain.title: Work, graphs and units
explain.body: Work is a scalar quantity, so it has magnitude but no direction. The area under a force-distance graph represents work. The SI unit is the joule: 1 J = 1 N m.

explain.title: Energy
explain.body: Energy can be defined as the ability of a body to do work. Energy is a scalar quantity, and its SI unit is joule (J). When work is done, energy is transferred to the body on which the work is done.

explain.title: Kinetic energy
explain.body: The kinetic energy of a body is the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its motion. The work needed to stop a moving body equals its kinetic energy. For mass m and velocity v, Eₖ = ½mv².

explain.title: Potential energy
explain.body: Potential energy is defined as the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its position or deformation. A raised body has gravitational potential energy because work was done to lift it.

explain.title: Gravitational potential energy

explain.title: The law of conservation of energy
explain.body: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It may be transformed from one form to another, but the total amount of energy never changes.

explain.title: Energy during a fall
explain.body: At the top, a body at rest has potential energy mgh and no kinetic energy. As it falls, potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases. At point B, their sum is mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh.

explain.title: Energy at the ground and waste energy
explain.body: Just before hitting the ground, the body's potential energy is zero and its kinetic energy is mgh. On impact, energy is dissipated as heat and sound. During energy transfers, some energy may become waste energy because work is done against friction; it is not available for useful work.

explain.title: Fossil fuel energy
explain.body: Fossil fuel energy comes out from burning of oil, coal and natural gas. These materials are known as fossil fuels. Their burning gives out heat, which is used to generate steam. The steam runs turbines to produce electricity.

explain.title: Hydroelectric generation
explain.body: Hydroelectric generation is the electricity generated from the power of falling water. Water in a high lake or reservoir possesses gravitational potential energy stored in it. When water is allowed to fall from height, the potential energy is changed into kinetic energy. Running water rotates a turbine, which runs the electric generator.

explain.title: Solar energy
explain.body: The energy obtained from sunlight is referred to as solar energy. Solar cells, also known as photo voltaic cells, transform sunlight directly into electricity. A single cell gives very low voltage, so many cells are connected in series to form a solar cell panel.

explain.title: Geothermal energy
explain.body: This energy is known as geothermal energy which can be extracted to run electric generators. Cold water is pumped down to hot rocks, where it heats up and boils. The steam comes out through another hole and runs the generator.

explain.title: Biofuel energy
explain.body: It is that energy which is obtained from the biomass. Biomass consists of organic materials such as plants, waste foods, animals dung, sewage, etc. In a digester, micro-organisms break down biomass in the absence of oxygen to produce methane-rich biogas.

Do not mix up the roles of a turbine, generator and transformer: running water or steam turns the turbine, the generator produces electricity, and a transformer changes voltage.

notes.title: Work done by a force
notes.answer: Work is the product of the magnitude of force and the distance covered in the direction of force.
notes.explanation: In physics, work is done when a force moves an object through a distance. Only the part of the force in the direction of the object's motion does work. Work is measured in joules.
notes.simple: A force does work only when it moves something in the force's direction. A force sideways to the motion, or no movement at all, means no work by that force.
examples: A force of 10 N moves an object 3 m in the same direction: W = FS = 10 × 3 = 30 J.
A person carries a bag horizontally at a steady height. The supporting force is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so the work done by that force is zero.
steps: Identify the force, the distance moved and the angle between them.
Use W = FS when the force and displacement are in the same direction.
Use W = FS cos θ when the force makes an angle θ with the direction of motion.

notes.title: Kinetic and potential energy
notes.answer: Energy is the ability of a body to do work. Kinetic energy is due to motion; potential energy is due to position or deformation.
notes.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it is moving. Potential energy is stored energy due to a body's position or deformation. Near the Earth, a raised body's gravitational potential energy is found using Eₚ = mgh.
notes.simple: Energy is the ability to do work. Motion gives a body kinetic energy; height or deformation can give it potential energy.
examples: A moving truck has kinetic energy.
A block held above the ground has gravitational potential energy.

notes.title: Conservation of Energy
notes.answer: The total energy remains mgh while the body falls, assuming air resistance is negligible.
notes.explanation: As a body falls, its potential energy changes into kinetic energy. If air resistance is negligible, the total energy stays the same.
notes.simple: Energy changes form, but the total amount does not disappear. A falling object changes potential energy into kinetic energy.
examples: At point B, the body has potential energy mg(h − x) and kinetic energy mgx.
Just before the body reaches the ground, its potential energy is zero and its kinetic energy is mgh.
steps: At A, the body is at rest and has potential energy mgh.
As it falls to B, it loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy.
At B, E_p = mg(h − x) and E_k = mgx.
Add the two forms: E = mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh.
Just before reaching the ground, E_p = 0 and E_k = mgh.

notes.answer: Percentage efficiency = (Useful output energy / Total input energy) × 100.
notes.explanation: Efficiency compares the useful energy a system gives out with the energy put into it. Percentage efficiency is this ratio multiplied by 100. Some input energy is always wasted, so a real system cannot be 100% efficient.
notes.simple: Efficiency tells you what fraction of the input energy becomes useful output. Some energy is wasted, so the useful output is less than the input.
examples: If useful output energy is 1200 J and input energy is 2000 J, efficiency = 1200/2000 = 0.6, or 60%.

written.text: A box of mass 10 kg is pushed up along a ramp 15 m long with a force of 80 N. If the box rises up a height of 5 m, what is the efficiency of the system?
modelAnswer: Total input energy = work done on the box
Useful output energy = gravitational potential energy gained
= mgh = 10 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 5 m = 500 J
Percentage Efficiency = (Useful output energy / Total input energy) × 100
written.followUp: A box of mass 10 kg is pushed up along a ramp 15 m long with a force of 80 N. If the box rises up a height of 5 m, what is the efficiency of the system?

rubric.why: The useful output energy is the gravitational potential energy gained by the box.
rubric.how: Use mgh = 10 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 5 m = 500 J.

written.text: Q5.7. A girl is swinging on a swing. At the lowest point of her swing, she is 1.2 m from the ground, and at the highest point she is 2.0 m from the ground. What is her maximum velocity and where?
modelAnswer: Loss in potential energy = gain in kinetic energy
v = √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = 4 m s⁻¹, at the lowest position

rubric.how: Set mgh equal to ½mv² and rearrange.

rubric.description: State the maximum speed and where it occurs.
rubric.why: The answer needs both the maximum speed and its position.
rubric.how: Use g = 10 m s⁻² and identify the lowest point as the point of maximum speed.
